extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and applicants preparing ex parte appeal briefs to the PTAB (attorneys, agents, pro se appellants)
extracted.subtask_short: PTAB ex parte appeal brief drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and filing ex parte appeal briefs to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, including required parts of the brief, argument structure, procedural filing tools/pilots, and tactical considerations for showing examiner error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal brief tool (template and instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two parts to the appeal brief tool: 1. Word document template; 2. PDF instructions for completing the template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location: PTAB page on USPTO website (www.uspto.gov/patents/ptab), 'New to PTAB' page, and 'Preparing an ex parte appeal brief' page. Use the Word template and follow the PDF instruction document when drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing an appeal brief via EFS-Web
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing information and instructions are available on the 'Preparing an ex parte appeal brief' page for filing via EFS-Web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the USPTO's EFS-Web filing procedures linked on the Preparing an ex parte appeal brief page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required parts of an appeal brief
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal brief should include six parts: Summary of claimed subject matter; Real party in interest; Related appeals, interferences, and trials; Argument; Conclusion (optional); Claims appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each listed part is present where applicable; some parts (e.g., Summary) are optional for pro se appellants but may help the Board understand arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each of the rejected independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not required for pro se applicants but may help the Board; if included, identify for each claim element the supporting disclosure and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real party in interest statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement identifying the real party in interest at the time the appeal brief is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May include inventor and any entities with ownership rights (e.g., assignee). Must be updated if it changes during the proceeding (See 37 C.F.R. § 41.8). Example format provided (e.g., 'The real party in interest is The Great White Café LLC (Baja, California 21511)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Related appeals, interferences, and trials disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: List any prior or pending cases before the Board or a court that are related to the current appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A related case is based on a patent or application you own that would affect or be affected by the current appeal (e.g., a continuation). Examples: provide appeal numbers and prior decision dates, or state there are none to appellant’s knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument — primary purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the examiner’s decision to reject the pending claims is improper and should be reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument section is where appellant shows the examiner erred; structure and clarity are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument — preliminary steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Before drafting argument, review the prosecution history, decide which rejections and which claims to address, and identify your strongest arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and prioritize matters to address; do not assume unaddressed rejections can be raised later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument — strategic considerations (page limits and prioritization)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no limit on the number of pages, BUT clearer and more concise arguments improve chances of prevailing. Present your strongest arguments first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid diluting strong arguments with weaker ones. Any rejection or argument not addressed cannot be presented later on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument — suggested format for grounds of rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Address each ground of rejection under a separate heading; identify the ground by claim number, statutory basis, and references (if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example heading format: 'Whether claims 1-3 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Reference A in view of Reference B.' Use clear headings for each ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim grouping guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same argument applies to two or more claims, consider arguing the claims as a group under a single heading or sub-heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Present claim 1 argument in full and state that claims 2 and 3 are patentable for the same reasons presented for claim 1. Grouping saves repetition and highlights commonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguing claims separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a separate heading or sub-heading for any claim that you want the PTAB to consider separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate subheadings (e.g., A. Claims 1 and 2; B. Claim 3) and explain patentability for each claim you want individually considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of rejections to address
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner’s rejection will be based on statutory requirements for patentability: 35 U.S.C. § 101 (patent ineligibility/lack of utility), § 102 (lack of novelty), § 103 (obviousness), § 112 (inadequate disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: examiner’s objections are usually petitionable, not appealable (See Ex parte Frye (precedential)). Identify which statutory ground applies to each rejection you address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial burden of proof rests with the examiner to clearly state reasons for the rejection; after that burden is satisfied, it shifts to appellant to explain why the examiner erred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure arguments to show where the examiner failed to meet initial burden or to rebut the examiner’s stated reasons once they are set forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why — give reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: For any argument showing the examiner erred, always give reasons to support your position; simply stating the examiner erred is not persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated explanation ('Because, because, because') with record citations and reasoning to support each contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common arguments showing examiner error
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical bases to show error include: examiner misunderstood or mischaracterized the claimed invention or the pending claims; examiner misunderstood the cited prior art; examiner misunderstood the law or legal basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific explanations tied to specification, claim language, prosecution history, and legal standards to rebut each misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument: misunderstood the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain that the examiner’s characterization or interpretation of the claim language is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show what a person of ordinary skill would understand from the specification and identify specific portions that support your interpretation. Provide explicit contrasts with the examiner’s interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument: misunderstood the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the examiner’s understanding of a prior art reference is incorrect—e.g., why the examiner erred in finding the reference discloses or suggests a claim element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the reference and explain why it does not disclose the recited element(s), identifying specific passages or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument: misunderstood the law (legal application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain that the examiner has failed to correctly apply the law (for example, insufficient reasoning to combine references in an obviousness rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide legal reasoning and factual support showing why the examiner’s conclusions are legally deficient (e.g., lack of sufficient rationale to combine references or reliance on impermissible hindsight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct the Board’s attention to evidence in the record (e.g., affidavits/declarations from experts) that supports your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot add new evidence to the record for the first time with the appeal brief. Use existing record evidence and explain how it supports your position with examples of declaratory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case law
rubrics_metrics.description: If aware of PTAB or federal court precedent that supports your position, explain how the case applies to the facts and shows the examiner erred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the decision and analyze its relevance—show parallels in facts or legal holdings and explain why the precedent requires reversal or different treatment of the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion and claims appendix requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion should briefly explain the relief requested (e.g., reverse the examiner’s rejection). The appendix must include all claims on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix should not indicate prior amendments or reference non-admitted amendments and should start on a new page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic warning about unaddressed rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rejection that you decide not to address and any arguments you decide not to present cannot be presented later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make strategic choices about which rejections to challenge on appeal, since omissions are forfeitures for later appeal stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: LEAP (Legal Experience and Advancement Program) eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: LEAP is designed to aid development of patent practitioners; to qualify, a patent agent or attorney must have three or fewer substantive oral arguments in any federal tribunal (including PTAB) and seven or fewer years of experience as a licensed attorney or agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program aims to encourage diverse advocates to develop skills before the Board; LEAP eligibility is a defined numeric criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-Track Appeals Pilot Program (expedited appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-year pilot to expedite ex parte appeals before the PTAB; appellant can request the appeal be expedited by filing a petition and a fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn more at the provided USPTO link. Separate COVID-19 related pilot allows filing a petition WITHOUT a fee for COVID-related appeals.
